passage:
Dear Bhavna,
You mentored me at the incubator two years ago, so I hope it's okay to ask for help.
The handloom marketplace is still running. I've said "one more month" to myself since January. It's now August. Orders are down again, and I've put in the last of my own savings. Every time I think of stopping, I think of everything I've already put in, and I can't.
I think that's pride talking. And fear, honestly, of telling everyone I quit.
So I want to do this properly. Could you look at the numbers with me next week, as someone who isn't inside my head? Before we meet I'll write down, in advance, what has to be true by 31 October for me to continue: a number of repeat buyers, and monthly costs covered. If we don't hit it, I'll close it cleanly, with notice to our weavers.
I'd rather choose an ending than drift into one.
Gurpreet

qa.a: Since January; it's now August.

qa.q: What feelings does Gurpreet admit are behind the delay?
qa.a: Gurpreet admits pride and fear, especially fear of telling everyone about quitting after putting in so much.

qa.q: What steps does Gurpreet plan to stop drifting?
qa.a: Setting kill criteria in advance for 31 October, asking Bhavna as an outsider to review the numbers, and closing cleanly with notice to the weavers if needed.

qa.a: Bhavna may feel touched to be trusted and relieved that Gurpreet is ready to face the numbers honestly.

grounding: The protagonist keeps saying one more month; seeing pride and fear behind it, they set kill criteria in advance and ask a trusted outsider to review the numbers.

passage: "I kept the cloud-kitchen going for eleven months longer than I should have. I'm Afreen, by the way. Every month I told my friend Tanuja, 'Next month the orders will pick up.' They didn't. I'd put everything into it, and quitting felt like admitting I'd wasted two years. So I kept telling myself stories. Then one night Tanuja, who's an accountant, just asked, 'What number would make you stop?' I didn't have one. That shocked me. So we sat on her floor and wrote them down: if orders stay below a certain level for three months, or if I have to borrow again, I close. We picked a date. Tanuja checked the numbers with me every month, because I couldn't trust myself to. In March, we hit the stop line. I closed it on my own terms, paid everyone, and cried for a week. But I chose it. That mattered."

qa.q: What question did Tanuja ask Afreen?
qa.a: "What number would make you stop?"

qa.a: Afreen felt afraid and proud, unwilling to admit two years might have been wasted, so kept telling hopeful stories.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt watching Afreen's stories each month?
qa.a: Tanuja was probably worried and frustrated, but patient enough to ask a clear question and help check the numbers.

grounding: The protagonist kept a failing venture going out of pride and fear; a trusted outsider helped set stop criteria so the ending was chosen, not drifted into.

I'm Irfan, and last year a big electronics chain launched a phone-repair service that looked exactly like ours, same doorstep pickup, same three-day promise, at a lower price. I remember reading their ad in the metro and feeling my ears go hot. We'd built that in Lucknow over three years.
That week I wrote a long angry post about "corporate thieves". Mehak, my co-founder, read it before I hit send. "Who is this for?" she asked. I didn't have a good answer.
So we deleted it and called twenty of our regular customers instead. What did they value? Not the price. It was that our technicians explained the repair in Hindi, didn't upsell, and fixed old phones the chain refused to touch.
We doubled down on that. Old models. Plain explanations. Six months later, we'd lost some customers to the chain. But the ones who stayed brought their parents.

qa.q: How many regular customers did Irfan and Mehak call?
qa.a: Twenty of their regular customers.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when reading the competitor's ad in the metro?
qa.a: Irfan felt angry and wronged, ears going hot, after building the service over three years.

qa.q: Which choice helped more than the angry post, and why?
qa.a: Asking customers what they valued and focusing on it, old phones and plain explanations, which the chain couldn't easily copy.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt reading the angry post?
qa.a: Mehak was probably worried it would make them look bitter, and calm enough to ask who it was really for.

grounding: A bigger competitor copies the service at a lower price; the protagonist feels angry but focuses on what customers value and what cannot be copied.

Bhupen's diary, 14 Dec.
Worst quarter yet. Two clients gone, payroll barely met.
Sonali-ma'am called anyway. She's been my mentor since the college accelerator. She never once said "it'll be fine". Today she said, "Your pricing is too low and you know it. You're scared to raise it." That hurt. Also true.
She stayed on the call an hour. Didn't offer money. Didn't offer to fix anything. Just asked hard questions until I had my own answers.
Things I'm doing because of her:
- raising the price for new clients from January
- dropping the custom-app work that eats all our time
- sending her an update on the 31st, whatever happens
Also, I finally wrote her a proper thank-you. Not "thanks for everything". I wrote: "Thank you for telling me the pricing truth when I didn't want to hear it. That call changed our December."
Grateful. Still scared.

I'm Ojas, and for eight months I edited videos for Nandini's travel channel. She was friendly, full of plans. "When we get sponsors, you'll be our head of production." Meanwhile, each video went through eight or nine rounds of changes, and my invoices got paid forty days late, then sixty.
I kept thinking I was doing something wrong. If I were faster, better, maybe she'd be happier.
Looking back, what changed it was a friend who looked at my messages and said, "This isn't you failing. This is someone taking advantage."
So I wrote to Nandini: from next month, two rounds of changes per video, anything more at a set rate, half the fee in advance, and a simple contract. I kept it polite.
She said I'd changed. I said my terms had. She stopped working with me a month later. I was sad, and also relieved. My new clients sign the contract without blinking.

qa.a: Forty days late, then sixty.

qa.a: Ojas felt anxious and inadequate, believing the endless changes and late payments were a personal failing.

Coaching note, session 4.
Pooja arrived late, eyes red. She runs a four-person design studio in Pune, and Zubin's retail chain is half her income. Last week Zubin asked for fifty store banners in three days. She said yes. She also said yes to a new website "by month end" and weekend calls.
She has slept five hours a night for two weeks. Two banners went out with the wrong prices, and Zubin was angry anyway.
She said, "If I say no, he'll leave. Then what?"
I asked what she could actually deliver well. She worked it out: twenty banners in three days, the rest by next Wednesday; the website in six weeks, not four. We practised how to say it: "Here's what I can do well, and when."
We also talked about finding two smaller clients over the next few months, so one client doesn't hold her whole studio.
She called Zubin from my office. He agreed to the new dates.

qa.a: Half her income.

qa.a: She was afraid of losing him, and worried that without Zubin the studio would not survive.

qa.q: What did the coach help Pooja do?
qa.a: Work out what she could deliver well, practise offering realistic timelines, and plan to find two smaller clients over time.

I'm Vandana, and my first big home-staging client, Sabina, nearly broke me. Three days after I finished her flat for sale, she messaged: "I'll only release the final payment if you also style my sister's flat. Otherwise, my review will say you're unprofessional."

The client review at the Chennai warehouse had already run two hours over, and the air-conditioning had died. Sarita, the project lead, watched Mr Iyer, the client's operations head, jab a finger at Ujjwal, her newest analyst. "Who taught you to make charts? A child could do better."
Ujjwal's ears went red. The room fell silent. The contract renewal was due next month.
Sarita felt a hot flash of anger and a cold flash of fear. She could let it pass. The renewal mattered.
She stood up. "Mr Iyer, could we take five minutes? Just you and me."
In the corridor, she said calmly, "I'm happy to hear any criticism of the work. I'll take it myself. But I'd ask you not to speak to my team that way."
Mr Iyer shrugged. "Fine."
Back inside, Sarita said, "Ujjwal's analysis is what our recommendation rests on. Ujjwal, walk us through slide four." His voice shook at first, then steadied.

qa.a: "Who taught you to make charts? A child could do better."

qa.q: How did Sarita protect Ujjwal?
qa.a: She spoke to Mr Iyer privately to set a boundary on tone, then backed Ujjwal publicly by asking him to present slide four.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel when asked to walk through slide four?
qa.a: Ujjwal is shaken at first, but likely feels supported and more confident as his voice steadies.
